lead: This unit sizes the parts that hold machines together and the parts that store energy: bolts, welds, pins and cotters, rivets and adhesives, power screws, springs and flywheels. Each is designed the same way: find every way it can fail, write one stress for each, and make the weakest one strong enough. After it you can size a bolt group or weld under an eccentric load, design a knuckle joint, cotter joint, riveted joint and screw jack, and design helical, concentric, leaf and rubber springs and a flywheel for a given duty.
about: The first four chapters are joints. Threaded fasteners and welds share one method for eccentric loads: move the load to the centroid, split it into a direct part and a moment part, and add the two at the worst point. Knuckle and cotter joints and riveted joints are then designed failure mode by failure mode, and bonded joints show why adhesives are loaded in shear. Power screws turn torque into a large axial force through an inclined plane. The next four chapters store energy in springs: helical springs in torsion, nested springs and fatigue, leaf springs in bending and rubber springs in shear and compression. The unit ends with flywheels, which store energy in rotation and must survive their own centrifugal stress.

chapters.idea: An eccentric load on a bolt group is split into a direct share for every bolt and a moment share proportional to distance from the group centroid; the vector sum at the worst bolt sizes the fastener.
chapters.depth: Thread terms: major, pitch and minor diameter, pitch, lead, single and double start, ISO metric stress area. Preload and torque-tension relation T = K d F_i with K about 0.2. Bolted joint under shear and tension. Eccentric load in the plane: find centroid, primary force F/n, moment M about centroid, secondary force M r/Σr², then vector sum. Eccentric tension: bolt forces vary linearly with distance from the neutral axis. Use core or stress area, not nominal diameter. Some syllabi call this a bolt group under eccentric shear.

figure.title: Eccentric bolted bracket
figure.aria: An eccentric load is moved to the bolt centroid, split into direct and moment shares, and combined into the maximum bolt load.

chapters.example: A bracket has four bolts at the corners of a 100 mm × 200 mm rectangle. A vertical load F = 12 kN acts at e = 250 mm from the centroid along the long centre line. Find the maximum shear force in a bolt. Use coordinates (±50, ±100) mm; Σr² = 50 000 mm²; M = 12 000 × 0.25 = 3 kN·m; maximum secondary shear = 3×10⁶ × 111.8 / 50 000 = 6.71 kN; primary shear = 3 kN; maximum resultant ≈ 8.49 kN.
chapters.trap: Adding primary and secondary shears as scalars. They are vectors at an angle, so take components at the worst bolt. A second trap is using the nominal bolt diameter instead of the stress area.
chapters.prereq: Unit 1: direct shear, tension and eccentric loading; principal stresses.
chapters.leave: Fatigue of bolted joints to Unit 2; keys and shaft couplings to Unit 3; weld design to 4.2.

chapters.idea: A weld is sized by its throat area and weld-line second moment; direct, bending and torsional stresses are combined at the point farthest from the weld-group centroid.
chapters.depth: Butt and fillet welds; equal-leg fillet throat t = 0.707h; effective length; weld symbols only as needed to read a drawing. Axial load: direct stress P/(tL). Eccentric load in the plane: torsion T r/J_w plus direct P/A_w. Out-of-plane load: bending M y/I_w plus direct. Weld-line method for thin throat: treat the weld as a line, then multiply stress by throat thickness. Permissible stresses and factor of safety. Some syllabi call fillet throat the effective throat.

figure.title: Eccentric fillet weld
figure.aria: The weld group gives throat area and polar moment, which turn load and torque into direct and torsional shear at the critical weld point.

chapters.example: Two vertical parallel fillet welds, each 100 mm long with leg h = 6 mm, are 100 mm apart centre to centre. A vertical load P = 10 kN acts at e = 150 mm from the centroid. Find the maximum resultant weld stress. Throat area = 2 × 0.707 × 6 × 100 = 848 mm²; direct shear = 10 000/848 = 11.8 MPa; T = 10 000 × 150 = 1.5 kN·m; J ≈ 2.83×10⁶ mm⁴; at the top of one weld r = 70.7 mm, torsional shear = 1.5×10⁶ × 70.7 / 2.83×10⁶ = 37.5 MPa; vector sum ≈ 46.6 MPa.
chapters.trap: Using the weld leg h as the throat. For a fillet weld the throat is 0.707h, so stress is higher by about 41%. Also do not add direct and torsional shear algebraically.
chapters.prereq: Unit 1: bending and torsion; chapter 4.1 for resolving eccentric load into direct and moment parts.
chapters.leave: Weld fatigue to Unit 2; bolt preload to 4.1; detailed bracket design to a design project.

chapters.idea: A knuckle joint puts the pin in double shear and bearing, while a cotter joint puts the cotter in double shear and bearing; each part is sized by its own failure mode.
chapters.depth: Knuckle joint: rod, eye, fork, pin. Failure modes: rod tension, eye tearing, pin double shear, pin bending, eye and fork crushing. Cotter joint: socket, spigot, cotter, collar. Failure modes: rod tension, cotter double shear, cotter crushing, socket tearing, collar crushing. Use standard proportions where a syllabus asks, but derive the critical size from stress. Some syllabi call the knuckle pin a hinge pin.

figure.title: Knuckle joint sizing
figure.aria: The tensile load first sizes the rod, then the pin in double shear, then the bearing areas of eye, fork and cotter.

chapters.example: A knuckle joint carries a rod tension P = 50 kN. Allowable tensile stress is 60 MPa and allowable shear stress is 40 MPa. Find the rod diameter and the pin diameter for double shear. Rod: d = √(4P/(πσ_t)) = √(4×50 000/(π×60)) = 32.6 mm, choose 34 mm. Pin: dₚ = √(2P/(πτ)) = √(2×50 000/(π×40)) = 28.2 mm, choose 30 mm.
chapters.trap: Using single shear for the knuckle pin. The pin has two shear planes, so the area is 2 × πdₚ²/4. The rod diameter is not automatically the pin diameter.
chapters.prereq: Unit 1: tension, shear and bearing stress; factor of safety.
chapters.leave: Standard cotter proportions and tolerances to design-office practice; combined eccentric loads to 4.1 and 4.2.

chapters.idea: A power screw is an inclined plane wrapped round a cylinder: torque must overcome thread friction and raise the load, and efficiency and self-locking follow from the lead angle and friction coefficient.
chapters.depth: Square, trapezoidal and Acme threads; mean diameter d_m, lead l, helix angle α = tan⁻¹(l/(πd_m)). Torque to raise a square thread: T = W d_m/2 × (μ + tanα)/(1 − μ tanα). Lowering torque and self-locking condition μ ≥ tanα. Efficiency η = tanα(1 − μ tanα)/(tanα + μ). Collar friction. Nut bearing pressure and number of threads. Screw body under torsion plus compression; buckling check for long screws. Some syllabi call this a translational screw.

figure.aria: Efficiency rises with lead angle for a square thread with friction coefficient 0.15; the marked point is the worked screw at 4.55 degrees.

chapters.example: A square-thread power screw has mean diameter d_m = 24 mm, lead l = 6 mm, and raises W = 20 kN. The thread friction coefficient is μ = 0.15 and collar friction is neglected. Find the lead angle, raising torque, efficiency and whether it self-locks. tanα = 6/(π×24) = 0.0796, α = 4.55°. T = 20 000 × 0.012 × (0.0796 + 0.15)/(1 − 0.15×0.0796) = 55.8 N·m. η = 0.0796(1 − 0.15×0.0796)/(0.0796 + 0.15) = 0.342, or 34.2%. Self-locking because μ = 0.15 > tanα = 0.0796.
chapters.trap: Using the nominal diameter in place of mean diameter, and using lead in place of pitch for a single-start thread. For efficiency, many quick solutions omit the (1 − μ tanα) factor; use the exact form when the lead angle is not small.
chapters.prereq: Unit 1: friction, torsion and combined stress; chapter 4.1 for thread terms.
chapters.leave: Thread manufacturing and standards to workshop practice; long-column buckling detail to a strength-of-materials course.

chapters.idea: A helical compression spring wire carries torsion; a curvature correction gives the true shear stress, deflection follows from strain energy, and surge is resonance of the spring coils.
chapters.depth: Terms: wire diameter d, mean coil diameter D, spring index C = D/d, active coils N_a, pitch, solid length, free length. Wahl factor K_w = (4C − 1)/(4C − 4) + 0.615/C. Stress τ = K_w × 8WD/(πd³). Deflection δ = 8WD³N_a/(Gd⁴); rate k = Gd⁴/(8D³N_a). Energy stored. Buckling of long springs. Surge: natural frequency from wire and coil dimensions; keep operating frequency away from it and its harmonics. Some syllabi call surge spring vibration.

figure.aria: The Wahl factor falls as spring index rises; the marked point is the worked spring with index 8.33 and factor 1.176.

chapters.example: A helical compression spring has D = 50 mm, d = 6 mm, N_a = 10 active coils, G = 80 GPa, and carries W = 500 N. Find the Wahl factor, maximum shear stress, deflection and spring rate. C = 50/6 = 8.33; K_w = (4C − 1)/(4C − 4) + 0.615/C = 1.176; τ = 1.176 × 8×500×0.05/(π×0.006³) = 347 MPa; δ = 8×500×0.05³×10/(80×10⁹×0.006⁴) = 48.2 mm; k = 500/0.0482 = 10.4 N/mm.
chapters.trap: Using the uncorrected stress 8WD/(πd³) and forgetting the Wahl factor. Also use mean coil diameter D, not outside diameter, in C and in deflection.
chapters.prereq: Unit 1: torsion of a wire and strain energy; Unit 2: fatigue background for 4.6.
chapters.leave: Fatigue design of springs to 4.6; detailed surge control hardware to a vibrations course.

chapters.idea: Concentric springs share a load by equal deflection, not equal load; fatigue design replaces static stress by mean and alternating shear compared with an endurance limit.
chapters.depth: Concentric or compound springs: two or more springs inside one another, same free length, opposite hand, clearance between coils. Equal deflection δ gives P₁/P₂ = k₁/k₂ and k_total = k₁ + k₂. Check solid height and clash. Fatigue: mean and alternating shear from fluctuating load; use Goodman or Soderberg with torsional endurance limit; Wahl factor on both components; stress concentration and shot peening; preset springs. Some syllabi call concentric springs nested springs.

figure.aria: Load rises linearly with deflection for each spring; at 150 mm the outer carries 7500 N, the inner 4500 N, and the pair carries 12 kN.

chapters.example: Two concentric springs share a total load W = 12 kN. The outer spring rate is k₁ = 50 N/mm and the inner rate is k₂ = 30 N/mm. Find the common deflection and the load in each spring. k_total = 50 + 30 = 80 N/mm; δ = 12 000/80 = 150 mm; P₁ = 50×150 = 7500 N; P₂ = 30×150 = 4500 N.
chapters.trap: Splitting the total load equally between concentric springs. They have the same deflection, so the stiffer spring carries more load. Also check that the inner spring has room to deflect without coil clash.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 4.5 for helical spring stress, rate and Wahl factor; Unit 2 for S-N curve and Goodman line.
chapters.leave: Manufacture of nested springs to workshop practice; fatigue of non-spring elements to Unit 2.

chapters.idea: A laminated leaf spring is a set of graduated strips clamped at the centre; it behaves as a beam of near-constant strength, so stress and deflection depend on the number, width and thickness of leaves.
chapters.depth: Semi-elliptic, quarter-elliptic and full-elliptic forms; master leaf, graduated leaves, central clamp, eyes, rebound clips. Nipping pre-stresses shorter leaves. For a semi-elliptic spring with span 2L, end load W (central load 2W), n leaves, width b, thickness t: σ = 6WL/(nbt²); δ = 6WL³/(E n b t³). Constant-strength argument and why graduated leaves save weight. Some syllabi call this a carriage spring.

figure.aria: Eight leaves are stacked, with the master leaf on top and shorter graduated leaves below, clamped at the centre.

chapters.example: A semi-elliptic leaf spring has span 1000 mm between eye centres, central load 5 kN, n = 8 leaves, b = 75 mm, t = 8 mm, E = 200 GPa. Find the maximum stress and deflection. Half-span L = 0.5 m; end load W = 2.5 kN; σ = 6×2500×0.5/(8×0.075×0.008²) = 195 MPa; δ = 6×2500×0.5³/(200×10⁹×8×0.075×0.008³) = 30.5 mm.
chapters.trap: Using the full span as L in the formula. The equations use half the eye-to-eye span and the load at one eye when the central load is 2W. Also use total leaves n, not only graduated leaves.
chapters.prereq: Unit 1: bending of beams and strain energy; chapter 4.5 for spring energy comparison.
chapters.leave: Vehicle suspension dynamics to an automotive course; fatigue of leaf springs to Unit 2.

chapters.idea: A flywheel stores energy as rotating inertia; the allowable speed fluctuation fixes the inertia, and centrifugal stress in the rim limits how fast a rimmed wheel can run.
chapters.depth: Coefficient of fluctuation of speed C_s = (ω₁ − ω₂)/ω and energy ΔE = Iω²C_s. Solid disk: I = ½mr². Rimmed wheel: I ≈ mr² for a thin rim. Rim hoop stress σ = ρv² for a free thin ring; v = ωr. Arms transmit torque from hub to rim and carry bending plus centrifugal tension. Stresses in rims and arms for engines and presses. Some syllabi call the rimmed flywheel a spoked flywheel.

figure.title: Rimmed flywheel check
figure.aria: The energy fluctuation and mean speed give inertia, then rim mass and rim speed give the centrifugal hoop stress.

chapters.example: A rimmed flywheel absorbs ΔE = 15 kJ per cycle at mean speed N = 600 rpm with C_s = 0.05. The rim mean radius is 0.6 m and cast iron density is 7200 kg/m³. Find the inertia, rim mass and hoop stress. ω = 2π×600/60 = 62.83 rad/s; I = ΔE/(ω²C_s) = 15 000/(62.83²×0.05) = 76.0 kg·m²; m = I/r² = 76.0/0.6² = 211 kg; v = ωr = 37.7 m/s; σ = ρv² = 7200×37.7² = 10.2 MPa.
chapters.trap: Using diameter in place of radius, and using the full speed change instead of the coefficient C_s. For a rimmed wheel, do not use the solid-disk inertia ½mr² unless the wheel really is a solid disk.
chapters.prereq: Unit 1: centrifugal force and thin-ring stress; chapter 4.7 for energy storage comparison.
chapters.leave: Engine balancing and torsional vibration to a later course; flywheel casting and inspection to manufacturing.
